title: Still No Cause, and Businesses Are Bleeding: The DoubleTree Fire Two Weeks Later

content:
Twelve days after a three-alarm fire ripped through Laredo’s DoubleTree by Hilton, two things remain true: nobody has told the public how the fire started, and the streets around the building are still closed — strangling the small businesses caught inside the perimeter.

The fire broke out around 12:52 a.m. on Wednesday, October 7, at the 14-story hotel at 800 Garden St., off I-35. More than 100 guests were evacuated in the middle of the night; seven to eight people were hospitalized for smoke inhalation. No one died. Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño declared a local state of disaster that morning, citing a possible collapse — officials had seen cracks in parts of the structure — and ordered surrounding streets shut: Constantinople, Garden, San Bernardo, and the I-35 frontage road.

The demolition warning

Over the weekend, Treviño said he met with the city manager, set deadlines for certain actions, and remains in communication with the hotel’s ownership. His message was blunt:

“The building’s structural integrity has been called into question, and I have been informed that ownership is pursuing efforts to reinforce and stabilize it. These efforts are time-sensitive and must be evaluated by qualified structural engineers to determine whether the building can be made safe.”

“If the building cannot be safely stabilized, we must move forward with a planned and coordinated demolition through the appropriate process. The City cannot allow an unsafe structure to continue placing people at risk.”

The mayor’s local disaster declaration ran from October 7 through October 14. Its current status is unclear — worth asking about at the next council meeting.

The businesses nobody is rescuing

While engineers debate the building’s bones, the neighbors are paying the price. Rolando Sauceda, who has run his restaurant on Constantinople Street for 32 years, told KGNS that sales have cratered with foot traffic cut off. He sympathizes with businesses that still can’t open and wants the city to help cover their costs while closures remain. A nearby resident, Julian Gonzalez, told reporters the building is unstable and asked that the closure perimeter be moved closer to the hotel so residents can move more freely.

What Webb Watch 956 is asking

  • The cause. It has been nearly two weeks. The fire is “under investigation” — but investigations have timelines, and the public deserves one.
  • The disaster declaration. It expired October 14. Was it extended? Under what authority are the streets still closed?
  • Business relief. Is the city considering any help — fee waivers, a relief fund — for the businesses the closures are choking? Sauceda asked. Nobody has answered yet publicly.
  • The stabilization clock. Ownership is “pursuing” stabilization. The mayor called it “time-sensitive” and set deadlines. What are the deadlines?
  • Who pays for demolition if it comes to that — the owner, or the taxpayers?

The DoubleTree reopened in 2025 after a roughly $10 million conversion. A demolished hotel is not just a lost building; it’s a hole in downtown’s tax base and a question mark over a marquee property. We covered the saga in full on October 18; this story will stay open until the questions are answered.
